chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad from someone else from Aban from Ibn Abi Yafur from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:

When they differ regarding the mortgage, one of the two says, 'I mortgaged it for a thousand dirhams,' and the other says, 'For one hundred dirhams,' then he (peace be upon him) said: 'The owner of the thousand is asked for proof. If he does not have proof, the owner of the hundred swears an oath.'

And if the mortgage item is less than what was mortgaged or more, and they differ, one says, 'It is a mortgage,' and the other says, 'It is a trust with you,' then he (peace be upon him) said: 'The owner of the trust is asked for proof. If he does not have proof, the owner of the mortgage swears an oath.'
ai.seo_question: How does Islamic jurisprudence resolve disputes over mortgage amounts and collateral status when parties disagree?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'al-bara'a al-awliya' (presumption of innocence) applied to financial disputes, where the burden of proof falls on the claimant of a higher obligation or specific status. It highlights the practical application of oath-swearing (yamin) as a secondary evidentiary tool when documentary evidence is lacking, ensuring equitable resolution between creditor and debtor. The hadith reflects the Imams' emphasis on clarity in contracts to prevent exploitation and maintain social justice in commercial dealings.
